1016.title: Ambedkar's vows
1016.hook: his twenty-two vows, and a Buddhism centered on equality
1016.howItsDone: At conversion ceremonies in the Ambedkarite tradition, new Buddhists take the three refuges and the five precepts and then recite Ambedkar's twenty-two vows together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the refuges at Nagpur, led by one of the crowd's own. Your line was dignity chosen.

After the refuges, Ambedkar didn't step down. The crowd was still standing on the open ground in Nagpur. He read out a list of vows, twenty-two of them, and asked them to take every one with him, line by line. Some sound like what anyone taking refuge might promise: keep the precepts, follow the eightfold path. Others are sharp, and meant to be. Running through the whole list, like a spine, is one idea: every person is equal.
screen: `A LIST OF VOWS.` → `SOME FAMILIAR, SOME SHARP.` → `ONE SPINE: EQUAL.`

segments.voice: First, the vows that turn away. A number of them ask his followers to leave behind the gods, rites and caste customs of the faith they were born into. Those vows were written for his own followers, out of his history and theirs, and Hindu readers may see them very differently. This lesson simply says what they say, and judges no one. Second, the vows that turn toward. Others commit to the Buddha's teaching: to keep the precepts, not to kill, steal or lie, to practice compassion and loving-kindness, and to walk the eightfold path. These would sound familiar in a monastery in Burma or Thailand. Third, rivers into the ocean. Among the vows is a plain statement that all people are equal, and a promise to work to make that true. An old picture in the Pali texts fits it. The Buddha compares the great rivers that flow into the ocean and lose their names there to people of every caste who join his order: once inside, the old names no longer count. Ambedkar read the Buddha's community in that spirit, as a place where caste dissolves. Fourth, a Buddhism for now. His followers sometimes call this reading Navayana, a new vehicle: the Buddha's path as freedom inside the mind and also freedom in society. Some Buddhists of other schools question parts of his reinterpretation; his followers hear in it the Buddha speaking straight into their lives. Either way, in these vows equality isn't only a feeling. It's a promise you say out loud.
screen: `SOME VOWS TURN AWAY.` · `SOME VOWS TURN TOWARD.` · `RIVERS LOSE THEIR NAMES.` · `EQUALITY AS A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three people: someone you look up to, someone you barely notice, and someone you find hard. See each as a river with its own name, running toward the same wide sea, and with each out-breath let the names soften until all three rest level in the water. You don't have to like them all; just see them as equal for a moment.
Ambedkar's vows. The twenty-two vows he gave at Nagpur, turning away from caste and toward the Buddha's path, with equality running through them. Today's word.
Your line: equal. Rivers lose their names in the sea. Day one thousand sixteen, done.

1017.title: The nuns return
1017.hook: since the late twentieth century, full ordination for women has been renewed in several lineages; views on it differ
1017.carry: taking the old story at its word
1017.howItsDone: In some Theravada and Mahayana communities women now receive full bhikkhuni ordination from monks and nuns together; in others women live as eight- or ten-precept nuns, and the question of renewal is discussed openly and settled differently by different communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ambedkar's vows, a Buddhism built on equality for everyone. Your line: equal.

Shaved heads, robes the color of turmeric, a line of women walking slowly into an ordination hall while monks wait inside to receive them. Scenes like this have happened in Sri Lanka, in Thailand, in the West, and each one has made news inside the Buddhist world. Why? Women have shaved their heads and kept precepts in Buddhist countries for a long time. But a fully ordained nun, a bhikkhuni, is something else. In some lineages that order had disappeared, and nobody alive could pass it on.
screen: `WOMEN WALK INTO THE HALL.` → `WHY IS THIS NEWS?` → `A LINE THAT HAD BROKEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the old story. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, Mahapajapati, the woman who raised the Buddha, asks him to let women go forth. He hesitates. She and other women cut their hair, put on robes and follow him anyway, on foot, until their feet are swollen and dusty. Ananda speaks for them and asks whether women can reach awakening. The Buddha says they can. So the order of nuns begins, with extra rules that place the nuns under the monks. Here's the difficulty. Full ordination is handed on by people who already have it, monks and nuns together. In the Theravada lands, the nuns' order died out or never took firm root, and in Tibet it seems never to have been brought in at all. Women kept practicing, as eight-precept or ten-precept nuns, without full ordination. Then, in our own time, women from Sri Lanka, Thailand and elsewhere received full ordination, sometimes with help from Chinese and Korean nuns, whose line had continued. Views differ, and the people who hold them are sincere. Some Theravada monks and scholars say a broken line can't be restored from outside, so these ordinations don't count under the rules. Others say the Buddha himself opened the door to women, and the rules allow it to be opened again. Tibetan teachers have studied the question at length. Some nuns are glad to keep their present vows and want no change. It's a real argument about keeping faith with rules handed down from teacher to student. And whatever any monastery decides, the women walking into those halls are taking the old story at its word.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `ORDINATION PASSES PERSON TO PERSON.` · `THE NUNS' LINE BREAKS, THEN RETURNS.` · `SINCERE VIEWS ON BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `WOMEN CAN AWAKEN.`

1018.title: Dipa Ma
1018.hook: the Indian laywoman who lost her family, found peace through meditation, and taught many
1018.howItsDone: Insight meditation teachers often tell Dipa Ma's story as an example of a householder's practice, and some retreat centers and sitting groups encourage people to bring noting into chores, cooking and caring for family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhikkhuni, women walking back into the ordination hall. Your line: taking the old story at its word.

A small woman in a white sari sits in a cramped apartment in Calcutta. Her visitors are students, neighbors, sometimes Westerners who've traveled a long way. She isn't a nun. She has no temple. She cooks, looks after her grandson, and teaches meditation from the floor of her home. Years earlier, people who knew her say, grief had left her so weak she could barely climb the steps of a temple. How did she get from there to here?
screen: `A WHITE SARI, A SMALL APARTMENT.` → `NO TEMPLE, NO ROBES.` → `ONCE TOO WEAK TO CLIMB THE STEPS.`

segments.voice: Her name was Nani Bala Barua, and people came to call her Dipa Ma, mother of Dipa, after her daughter. She grew up in a Buddhist family in Bengal, married, and moved with her husband to Burma. Then the losses came, one after another, as her students tell it: children who died, and then her husband. She was left with her young daughter Dipa, with grief, and with a failing body. A doctor, the story goes, told her that her real illness was sorrow, and that she should learn to meditate. So she went to a meditation center in Rangoon. The early days were hard. On her way there, her students say, she would stop and stop, and finally crawl up the stairs. But she kept going. She practiced noting, naming each movement of body and mind as it happened, and over time, they say, the grief loosened its hold and her health came back. Later she taught in Calcutta, mostly householders like herself: mothers, workers, people who couldn't leave for a monastery. Some of the teachers who later brought insight meditation to the West studied with her. What she told them was plain. Practice in the kitchen: while you cook, while you wash, while you look after a child. You don't need a cave. And notice the order of the story. She didn't heal first and then practice. She practiced while she was broken, and rebuilt from there, one noted step at a time.
screen: `NANI BALA BARUA, CALLED DIPA MA.` · `LOSS AFTER LOSS, THEN ILLNESS.` · `CRAWLING UP THE STAIRS TO PRACTICE.` · `TEACHING HOUSEHOLDERS IN CALCUTTA.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who went through something hard and slowly put a life back together: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, maybe you. Don't retell the whole story; just picture them on an ordinary day afterward, making breakfast, laughing at something small, and let the respect be quiet. If your mind drifts, note it, wandering, and come back to their face.
Dipa Ma. A laywoman who practiced through grief, rebuilt her life, and taught householders to meditate right where they lived.
Your line: she rebuilt. Practice can start in the kitchen, even on a broken day. See you tomorrow.

1019.title: Engaged Buddhism
1019.hook: Thich Nhat Hanh and others bring practice to war, peace and daily life
1019.howItsDone: Engaged Buddhist groups run prison meditation programs, hospice care, disaster relief and peace work, and communities in the Plum Village tradition practice mindful breathing and walking alongside their service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dipa Ma, practicing through grief and teaching from her kitchen floor. Your line: she rebuilt.

A temple bell rings for evening sitting. Outside, not far off, there's the sound of planes, and smoke over a village. Inside the temple, young monks look at each other. This was Vietnam during the war, and the question in that room was not abstract. Do you stay on the cushion, where the practice is? Or do you go out to the village, where the people are? A monk named Thich Nhat Hanh spent his life answering that, and the answer gave a name to a whole movement.
screen: `A BELL, AND SMOKE OVER A VILLAGE.` → `STAY ON THE CUSHION?` → `OR GO OUT?`

segments.voice: Thich Nhat Hanh was a Vietnamese Zen monk. As he told it later, when bombs were falling, monks and nuns had to choose between meditating in the monastery and going out to help the wounded. He said they chose both. They rebuilt villages and cared for people, and kept their mindfulness while they did it, breathing as they carried the injured, walking with attention through the ruins. He called this engaged Buddhism: practice that doesn't stop at the temple door. He started a school of young social workers who went into the villages. He spoke against the war, was barred from going home, and lived much of his life in exile, teaching in France. He wasn't the only one. Teachers in other countries have brought the practice into prisons, hospitals, protests, refugee camps and kitchens, each in their own way. Here's the turn that keeps it Buddhist: it isn't only what you do, but how. For Thich Nhat Hanh, anger at injustice was real, but acting from anger, he said, only adds more of the same to the world. So the work starts inside: a breath before the meeting, attention while you wash the dishes, listening fully to someone you disagree with. Then you go out. Not everyone in the tradition draws the lines the same way; some teachers keep monks far from politics, others step into it. But the root is old. The Buddha taught that compassion, karuna, is one of the qualities a practitioner grows. Engaged Buddhism asks where that compassion goes when you stand up from the cushion.
screen: `MONKS CHOOSE: CUSHION OR VILLAGE?` · `THEY CHOSE BOTH.` · `NOT ONLY WHAT YOU DO, BUT HOW.` · `COMPASSION OFF THE CUSHION.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Choose one real thing that's wrong, in your house, your street, your town, small enough to hold, and notice what comes up: frustration, maybe tiredness. Breathe with that for a moment without pushing it away. Then ask quietly what one thing you could do about it, from a calm place rather than an angry one, and let an answer come, or not.
Engaged Buddhism. Practice carried out of the temple and into war, peace and daily life, with attention to how the work is done.
Your line: practice in the world. Not only what you do, but how. That's day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: The Fourteenth Dalai Lama
1020.hook: a monk and teacher in exile since 1959, known for kindness as his religion
1020.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists attend the Dalai Lama's public teachings in Dharamsala and elsewhere, and practice compassion trainings in which they reflect that all beings want happiness and do not want suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday: engaged Buddhism, monks who left the cushion for the village and kept practicing as they worked. Your line: practice in the world.

Ask him what he is, and the answer usually comes back simple: a Buddhist monk. Not a king, not a god-king, not a celebrity, though his face hangs in homes and on posters. A monk who gets up early, sits, studies and recites, the way monks in his tradition do. He laughs a lot in interviews, and he keeps bringing the conversation back to one thing. When people ask about his religion, he has said it is very simple: kindness.
screen: `A SIMPLE BUDDHIST MONK.` → `MAROON ROBES, AN EASY LAUGH.` → `HIS RELIGION: KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: In Tibetan Buddhism, his followers understand the Dalai Lama as a teacher who returns, life after life, as an emanation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Tradition says that when one Dalai Lama dies, senior lamas search for the child in whom he has returned, using signs, visions and tests. The present Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, is the fourteenth in that line. He was found as a small boy in a farming village and brought to Lhasa to be trained. During the Chinese takeover of Tibet, he fled across the mountains into India. He has lived there ever since, with a community of Tibetans around him in Dharamsala, teaching, writing and meeting people from everywhere. Not everyone sees him the same way. For Tibetans who follow him he is a spiritual guide and a symbol of home. The government of China disputes his role. Some Tibetan Buddhists follow other lamas first. Here, though, the interest is what he teaches. He studied the long, hard texts of Tibetan philosophy and earned the geshe degree, a title for monk-scholars. Yet with wide audiences he keeps returning to compassion and kindness, which he calls the root of the practice, and he says these don't belong to Buddhists alone. Kindness, as he describes it, isn't softness. It's training: noticing that other people want happiness and don't want to suffer, just as you do, and letting that change how you act. Practiced again and again, until it becomes habit. That's what turns kindness from a mood into a practice.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO RETURNS.` · `FOUND AS A CHILD, TRAINED IN LHASA.` · `EXILE IN INDIA.` · `KINDNESS AS TRAINING, NOT A MOOD.` · then, large: `THEY WANT HAPPINESS TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today, not your favorite person, just someone, and say quietly: this person wants to be happy, just like me; this person doesn't want to suffer, just like me. Then try the same two lines with someone who annoys you. Don't force a warm feeling; just notice what the words do.
Tenzin Gyatso, the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, a Tibetan monk and teacher living in exile, who calls kindness the heart of his practice.

1021.title: Peace walks
1021.hook: Maha Ghosananda leads peace walks across Cambodia after the killing years
1021.howItsDone: In Cambodia, the Dhammayietra peace walks continued after Maha Ghosananda, and Buddhists elsewhere practice walking meditation, sometimes walking together in silence for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tenzin Gyatso, a monk in maroon who calls kindness his practice. Your line: kindness as practice.

A dirt road in Cambodia. At the front, a small, elderly monk in saffron, walking slowly, sometimes smiling, sometimes sprinkling water from a bowl on the people who kneel by the road. Behind him, a long line: monks, nuns, laypeople, some carrying flags, some barefoot. The fields they pass have seen terrible things; in some places there are still mines in the ground. Nobody in the line is armed. They're walking through a country torn apart by its own government, and they're walking for peace.
screen: `A DIRT ROAD, A SMALL MONK.` → `A LONG LINE BEHIND HIM.` → `NO ONE ARMED.`

segments.voice: His name was Maha Ghosananda, a Cambodian monk, and he was living abroad when the Khmer Rouge came to power. Under that regime, temples were emptied, monks were killed or forced out of their robes, and Cambodians died in the fields and in the prisons. His students say his own family was among those lost. When the killing years ended, he went to the refugee camps along the Thai border and set up simple temples among the tents. There, people say, he chanted one verse from the Dhammapada again and again. In Max Müller's old translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." He said it to people who had lost everything to hatred. Not to excuse what happened, but because, as he saw it, more hatred would only start the circle again. Later, back in Cambodia, he began leading walks for peace, the Dhammayietra, a pilgrimage of the Dhamma, through regions where fighting hadn't fully stopped. People came out of their villages to meet the walkers with water and incense. Some walkers were hurt along the way. Still they walked. His way of putting it was plain: peace is made step by step, slowly, the way you walk. Each step can be a kind of meditation, and each meditation a step toward peace. He didn't promise it would be quick. He promised it would be walked.
screen: `THE KILLING YEARS.` · `CHANTING IN THE REFUGEE CAMPS.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE DHAMMAYIETRA: WALKING FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and take one unhurried step, then another, at the pace of someone in a long line; if you're seated, press each foot gently into the floor in turn. Let one quiet word ride along with each step: peace, not as a demand, more like company. If your mind runs ahead to your list, come back to the next step; there's nowhere to arrive.
Peace walks. The Dhammayietra, Maha Ghosananda's walks through a wounded Cambodia, made one slow step at a time.
Your line: step by step, peace. Hatred ceases by love, one step at a time. Day one thousand twenty-one, done.

chat.says: After so much killing, how could a monk tell survivors to stop hating?
options: He chanted that hatred never ends hatred; more of it only starts the circle again.
He told them what happened didn't matter, and they should simply forget it.
He told them to hate only the leaders, since well-aimed hatred brings peace.
chat.meaning: Maha Ghosananda chanted Dhammapada 5: hatred ceases by love. He didn't excuse what happened; he saw that more hatred would only start the circle again.

1022.title: Women teaching today
1022.hook: across every school, women lead temples and teach
1022.howItsDone: Women lead Buddhist temples, monasteries, retreat centers and sitting groups in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana communities, giving dharma talks and training students; some communities restrict certain roles.

segments.voice: Yesterday: peace walks, a long, unarmed line behind Maha Ghosananda. Your line: step by step, peace. And the week behind it: equal, bhikkhuni, she rebuilt, practice in the world, kindness as practice.
screen: `STEP BY STEP, PEACE.` → `EQUAL.` · `BHIKKHUNI.` · `SHE REBUILT.` · `PRACTICE IN THE WORLD.` · `KINDNESS AS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Long ago, the story goes, a nun named Soma sat down under a tree to meditate, and Mara, the tempter, came to shake her. A woman, he sneered, with her little bit of sense, can't reach what the sages reach. Soma didn't argue about women. She asked a better question: what does being a woman matter, when the mind is steady and wisdom is there? Mara, seen through, disappeared. That conversation is very old. It's still going, and women are the ones answering.
screen: `SOMA UNDER A TREE.` → `MARA SNEERS.` → `WHAT DOES IT MATTER, IF THE MIND IS STEADY?`

segments.voice: Soma's verses survive in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, poems by early Buddhist women about their own awakening. So women's voices are in the old canon itself. Now look across the schools in recent times. In the Theravada world, a German-born nun named Ayya Khema taught widely and helped found a place for nuns on an island in Sri Lanka. In Tibetan Buddhism, Tenzin Palmo, an English-born nun, spent years on retreat in a Himalayan cave and later built a nunnery where Tibetan nuns could study and practice. Pema Chodron, an American nun in the Tibetan tradition, became known for plain talk about fear and difficulty. In Taiwan, the nun Cheng Yen founded Tzu Chi, a Buddhist relief organization run largely by laypeople. In Zen and Korean Son, women serve as abbots and teachers, and lay women lead sitting groups in living rooms and community halls. They stand in different schools, with their own rules, and they don't all agree, including on the ordination questions from earlier this week. But look at what they do: they run temples, give dharma talks, lead retreats, train students, and some of their students are men. So Soma's question gets its answer in practice, not in debate. That doesn't erase the obstacles women have faced, and some communities still hold back certain roles. But the picture of Buddhist teachers as only old men in robes is out of date. Women are leading, right now, in the halls.
screen: `THE THERIGATHA: THE ELDER NUNS' VERSES.` · `AYYA KHEMA, TENZIN PALMO, PEMA CHODRON.` · `CHENG YEN AND TZU CHI.` · `ABBOTS, TEACHERS, GROUP LEADERS.` · then, large: `THEY LEAD.`

segments.voice: Bring Soma to mind under her tree, unbothered by the sneer, and borrow her question. As the mind hands you labels, woman or man, young or old, good at this or hopeless at it, ask each one: when the mind is steady, what does this matter? Don't argue with the label; just let it grow smaller than the breath.
Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, from Soma's verses in the canon to abbots, nuns and lay teachers across the schools now.
Your line: they lead. Soma's question still holds the floor. That's day one thousand twenty-two.

chat.says: Can women really be Buddhist teachers, or is it all men in robes?
options: Women teach across the schools now, and early nuns' own poems are in the canon.
Only in new Western groups; there have been no women teachers in Asia.
Women teach only in Taiwan; the other schools have no women teachers at all.
chat.meaning: Women's voices are in the old canon itself, the Therigatha, and today women run temples, lead retreats and train students, some of them men.
